title: Singular-value decomposition
subtitle: G2 lecture 036000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded companion deck developed from the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix. Adds explicit mathematical formulas, worked examples, and topic-specific diagrams while remaining standalone.

slides.title: Stretching in preferred directions
slides.lead: The singular-value decomposition finds orthogonal input directions that A stretches independently.
body: For a map A : E → F, the positive operator A* A lives on the source space E. Its eigenvectors give the right input directions, and the square roots of its eigenvalues give the stretch factors.
The SVD then manufactures matching orthogonal output directions so that A acts as “stretch by σ_i, then send v_i to u_i.”
slides.takeaway: The SVD diagonalizes stretching even when A itself is not self-adjoint or square.

slides.title: Start from the source Gram operator
slides.lead: Choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of A* A on the source space.
body: Because A* A is positive, all eigenvalues are nonnegative. Their square roots σ_i are called the singular values of A, and the eigenvectors v_i are the right singular vectors.
These vectors describe the source directions in which A acts most cleanly. They are orthogonal because A* A is self-adjoint.
slides.takeaway: Right singular vectors are just the orthonormal eigenvectors of A* A.

slides.title: Construct the output directions
slides.lead: For each positive singular value, push the input vector through A and normalize.
body: If σ_i > 0, then A v_i is nonzero and its norm is exactly σ_i. Dividing by σ_i produces a unit vector u_i in the target space F.
A short calculation shows that distinct u_i are orthogonal. These are the left singular vectors. They are the output directions paired with the right singular vectors.
slides.takeaway: The target directions arise canonically by normalizing the nonzero outputs A v_i.

slides.title: What if a singular value is zero?
slides.lead: Zero singular values correspond exactly to kernel directions.
body: If σ_i = 0, then A* A v_i = 0. The modulus identity implies ||A v_i||² = ⟨A* A v_i, v_i⟩ = 0, so A v_i = 0. Those right singular vectors span ker A.

There is no associated normalized output direction because the output is zero. We therefore complete the output side with any orthonormal basis of the orthogonal complement once the positive singular values have been handled.
slides.takeaway: Zero singular values mark the directions that A annihilates.

slides.title: The decomposition formula
slides.lead: With orthonormal families in hand, A decomposes into rank-one pieces.
body: Here r is the rank of A, the number of positive singular values. Each term v_i^* extracts the coefficient along the input direction v_i, multiplies it by σ_i, and places the result in the output direction u_i.
This is the coordinate-free content of the SVD. In matrix form it becomes A = U Σ V*.
slides.takeaway: Every linear map is a sum of orthogonal rank-one stretches.

slides.title: A complete example
slides.lead: Take A = diag(3,1) on the plane.
body: Because A is already positive diagonal, the right singular vectors are the coordinate axes, the left singular vectors are the same, and the singular values are 3 and 1. This is the easiest possible SVD.
Rotating the domain or codomain would change U and V, but the singular values would remain unchanged because they are intrinsic to A* A.
slides.takeaway: In a favorable basis the SVD is literally a diagonal stretch.

slides.title: Intrinsic data versus basis choices
slides.lead: Singular values are canonical; singular vectors may not be unique.
body: If a singular value has multiplicity one, its singular directions are determined up to sign or phase. If it has higher multiplicity, any orthonormal basis of the corresponding singular subspace may be used.
So the decomposition is not unique term by term inside repeated singular-value spaces, but the singular values and the associated source and target subspaces are intrinsic.
slides.takeaway: Repeated singular values create basis freedom but not ambiguity about the singular subspaces.

slides.title: How A* A and A A* are related
slides.lead: The nonzero spectra of A* A and A A* coincide.
slides.mathtex: A^*A v_i = \sigma_i^2 v_i,\qquad A A^* u_i = \sigma_i^2 u_i
body: The right singular vectors diagonalize A* A and the left singular vectors diagonalize A A*. Both operators therefore encode the same positive numbers σ_i², though on different spaces.
This explains why rank equals the number of positive singular values and why either side of the map can be used to recover the same stretching data.
slides.takeaway: The source and target Gram operators share the same nonzero singular-value information.

slides.title: Best approximation and norm information
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 036000 · Why the SVD is powerful
slides.lead: The singular values control many other matrix quantities.
body: The largest singular value is the operator norm. Partial sums of singular values govern Ky Fan norms, and truncating the SVD produces the best low-rank approximation in the Eckart–Young theorem.
So the decomposition is not just a convenient factorization. It is the main gateway to quantitative matrix analysis.
slides.takeaway: The SVD packages the stretching data that many later norm inequalities will use.

slides.title: Bridge to polar decomposition
slides.lead: The SVD already suggests the factorization A = U|A|.
body: The modulus |A| acts on each right singular vector by |A|v_i = σ_i v_i. A partial isometry then sends each surviving v_i to the corresponding u_i. In that way the SVD separates naturally into a positive stretch and a direction-preserving transport.
The next lecture extracts exactly that canonical factorization without committing to a full choice of singular bases.
slides.takeaway: Polar decomposition is the invariant core of the singular-value decomposition.
